## The same calculation, now from a file

```python
income = 1000
consumption = 800
print(income - consumption)
```

::: {.answer .fragment}
`200` EUR per month. We will obtain these inputs from a CSV, repeat the
calculation for four households, and check the results.
:::

::: {.notes}
Clock 01:00–03:00 (2 minutes). Connect the first and last blocks of the day. Ask students
what a row represents before discussing code. The goal is a checked result,
not merely opening a file. Later lessons add merging, cleaning and graphs.
:::

## A CSV is a plain-text table

An excerpt showing **three of the six columns**:

```{.text code-line-numbers="false"}
household_id,income_eur_month,consumption_eur_month
1,1000,800
2,1200,800
```

- The first line contains column names.
- Each subsequent line contains one household's values.
- Commas separate fields; they are not thousands separators here.

::: {.notes}
Clock 05:00–07:00 (2 minutes). Open the real CSV in a text editor without saving changes.
The complete file contains four data rows and also household_size, employed
and survey_year. This slide is explicitly an excerpt, not a different dataset.
Do not double-count the header as a household.
:::

## Define the observation and its units

```python
household_id = 4
income_eur_month = 800
consumption_eur_month = 850
print(income_eur_month - consumption_eur_month)
```

::: {.answer .fragment}
`-50` EUR per month: this household consumes more than its current income.
:::

One row is **one synthetic household in 2026**. Household size is persons;
`employed` is an invented `0`/`1` indicator.

::: {.notes}
Clock 07:00–09:00 (2 minutes). Read the column names as part of the data documentation.
There is no real population or sampling design behind this teaching fixture.
Negative saving is permitted. The binary employment indicator is supplied for
practice and should not be mistaken for a documented survey definition.
:::

## Import pandas once

```python
import pandas as pd

print("pandas is ready")
```

::: {.terminal-output}
```{.text code-line-numbers="false"}
pandas is ready
```
:::

**pandas** provides tools for tables. `pd` is the conventional short name used
throughout this notebook.

::: {.notes}
Clock 09:00–10:00 (1 minute). pandas is already in the course environment. An import makes
its tools available to this Python process; it does not install the package.
Do not change environments or install extra packages during the lesson.
Reference: https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/getting_started/intro_tutorials/02_read_write.html
:::

## Check the path, then read the CSV

```python
from pathlib import Path

data_path = Path("data/raw/households.csv")
print(data_path.is_file())
households = pd.read_csv(data_path)
print(type(households).__name__)
```

::: {.terminal-output .fragment}
```{.text code-line-numbers="false"}
True
DataFrame
```
:::

::: {.small-note}
If the file check is `False`, check your working folder and filename first.
The path is relative to the folder from which this notebook runs.
:::

::: {.notes}
Clock 10:00–13:00 (3 minutes). Explain read_csv as reading a table into a DataFrame. The
__name__ display is supplied so students see a short type label; memorising
that syntax is not required. Run setup cells before the later examples, which
reuse households. Use Path.cwd() to diagnose a path problem; do not edit the
CSV or insert a machine-specific absolute path into the shared notebook.
:::

## Look at a few rows before calculating

```python
columns = ["household_id", "income_eur_month",
           "consumption_eur_month"]
preview = households[columns]
print(preview.head(2).to_string(index=False))
```

::: {.terminal-output .fragment}
```{.text code-line-numbers="false"}
 household_id  income_eur_month  consumption_eur_month
            1              1000                    800
            2              1200                    800
```
:::

`head(2)` selects the first two rows for inspection. It does not remove the others.

::: {.notes}
Clock 13:00–15:00 (2 minutes). Explain that columns is an ordinary list of names; indexing
the DataFrame with that list selects columns. We use to_string only to keep
the printed slide output compact and consistent; a notebook can display
preview.head(2) directly. The full households DataFrame still contains six columns.
:::

## Count rows and columns

```python
print(households.shape)
print(len(households))
```

::: {.terminal-output .fragment}
```{.text code-line-numbers="false"}
(4, 6)
4
```
:::

::: {.definition}
`.shape` reports **(rows, columns)**. `len(...)` reports the number of rows here.
:::

::: {.notes}
Clock 15:00–17:00 (2 minutes). Ask students to explain why the CSV header does not create a
fifth row. The shape is for the unmodified households DataFrame. Later derived
columns will be stored in a separate working table called analysis.
:::

## Inspect the column names exactly

```python
for name in households.columns:
    print(name)
```

::: {.terminal-output .fragment}
```{.text code-line-numbers="false"}
household_id
income_eur_month
consumption_eur_month
household_size
employed
survey_year
```
:::

Spelling, underscores, and capitalisation matter when selecting a column.

::: {.notes}
Clock 17:00–19:00 (2 minutes). This reuses a for loop from the earlier block. Inspect names
before trying to guess them. A KeyError for a column often reflects a name
mismatch, but students should read the actual message before choosing a repair.
:::

## Inspect stored types and economic meaning

```python
columns = ["household_id", "income_eur_month"]
print(households[columns].dtypes.to_string())
```

::: {.terminal-output .fragment}
```{.text code-line-numbers="false"}
household_id        int64
income_eur_month    int64
```
:::

Both are stored as integers, but **an identifier is not an income measurement**.
The storage type alone does not tell you what a column means.

::: {.notes}
Clock 19:00–21:00 (2 minutes). Explain int64 simply as an integer storage type. Exact dtype
labels can differ for other inputs and environments. Averaging household IDs
would be meaningless even though pandas can add their numeric representations.
The fixture has only integer fields; real files can contain strings and missing values.
:::

## Select one column

```python
incomes = households["income_eur_month"]

print(type(incomes).__name__)
print(incomes.to_list())
```

::: {.terminal-output .fragment}
```{.text code-line-numbers="false"}
Series
[1000, 1200, 2000, 800]
```
:::

One selected column is a **Series**. `.to_list()` shows its values as a familiar list.

::: {.notes}
Clock 21:00–23:00 (2 minutes). A Series also has an index, which to_list omits. We are using
the list representation to connect to Basic Python, not discarding the index
throughout the analysis. Reference: https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/getting_started/intro_tutorials/03_subset_data.html
:::

## Select a table with two columns

```python
columns = ["household_id", "income_eur_month"]
selected = households[columns]

print(type(selected).__name__)
print(selected.shape)
```

::: {.terminal-output .fragment}
```{.text code-line-numbers="false"}
DataFrame
(4, 2)
```
:::

The selection uses a **list of column names**. It leaves the original table unchanged.

::: {.notes}
Clock 23:00–25:00 (2 minutes). Point out the difference between households["income_eur_month"]
and households[["income_eur_month"]]: the first is a Series, the second a
one-column DataFrame. Students need not memorise every return type today;
they should know how to inspect the object they have.
:::

## Select a row by its position

```python
first_household = households.iloc[0]

print(first_household["household_id"])
print(first_household["income_eur_month"])
```

::: {.terminal-output .fragment}
```{.text code-line-numbers="false"}
1
1000
```
:::

`.iloc[0]` selects the first row by **position**. Its household ID happens to be `1`.

::: {.notes}
Clock 25:00–27:00 (2 minutes). Position, index label and household identifier are different
concepts. Position starts at zero. Sorting a table could change which household
is first; position zero would still mean the first row of the current table.
:::

## Your turn · Predict three inspections

::: {.exercise}
1. Predict each output before running the code.
2. Run it and check your predictions.
3. Explain which expression selects rows and which selects columns.
:::

```python
print(households.shape)
print(households["income_eur_month"].iloc[-1])
print(households[["household_id", "employed"]].shape)
```

::: {.answer .fragment}
`(4, 6)`, then `800`, then `(4, 2)`.
:::

::: {.notes}
Clock 27:00–32:00 (5 minutes). Allow three minutes for prediction and running and two for
discussion. The .iloc[-1] expression selects the last income value; the list
of two names selects columns. Keep the input table unchanged.
:::

## Use a Boolean mask to select households

```python
employed = households["employed"] == 1
print(employed.to_list())
print(households.loc[employed, "household_id"].to_list())
```

::: {.terminal-output .fragment}
```{.text code-line-numbers="false"}
[True, True, True, False]
[1, 2, 3]
```
:::

The comparison produces **one Boolean per row**. `.loc[mask, column]` keeps rows
whose mask is `True` and selects the named column.

::: {.notes}
Clock 32:00–35:00 (3 minutes). The name employed is a Boolean Series here, while the column
employed contains the original 0/1 indicator. Trace the four comparisons by
hand. This is selection for a question, not an instruction to delete other
households from the source data.
:::

## Combine two column comparisons

```python
mask = ((households["employed"] == 1)
        & (households["income_eur_month"] >= 1200))

print(households.loc[mask, "household_id"].to_list())
```

::: {.terminal-output .fragment}
```{.text code-line-numbers="false"}
[2, 3]
```
:::

Use **`&`** between these pandas comparisons and put each comparison in parentheses.
Python's plain `and` is for the scalar Boolean questions shown earlier.

::: {.notes}
Clock 35:00–37:00 (2 minutes). Make the distinction explicit rather than implying that the
earlier and lesson was wrong. Each comparison here is a whole column of
Boolean values. Do not introduce complicated filters or operator precedence
rules beyond this parenthesised pattern.
:::

## Calculate saving for every row

```python
analysis = households.copy()
analysis["saving_eur_month"] = (
    analysis["income_eur_month"]
    - analysis["consumption_eur_month"]
)

print(analysis["saving_eur_month"].to_list())
```

::: {.terminal-output .fragment}
```{.text code-line-numbers="false"}
[200, 400, 500, -50]
```
:::

The subtraction works **row by row**. The raw CSV and `households` remain unchanged.

::: {.notes}
Clock 37:00–40:00 (3 minutes). Connect to the earlier loop over household inputs. pandas
expresses this column calculation without writing that loop ourselves. We use
a separate analysis table to distinguish inputs from derived values. The CSV
on disk changes only if code explicitly writes to its path.
Reference: https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/getting_started/intro_tutorials/05_add_columns.html
:::

## Check a row against a hand calculation

```python
fourth_household = analysis.iloc[3]
print(fourth_household["saving_eur_month"])

assert fourth_household["saving_eur_month"] == 800 - 850
```

::: {.terminal-output .fragment}
```{.text code-line-numbers="false"}
-50
```
:::

The fourth household's negative saving is an interpretable result.
An assertion should check the intended calculation, not forbid valid outcomes.

::: {.notes}
Clock 40:00–42:00 (2 minutes). Use exact equality for this integer example. A numerical
assertion passing for one row is evidence for that row, not a guarantee that
an entire real data pipeline is correct. Ask students to check the first row too.
:::

## Summarise with the denominator in mind

```python
print(analysis["saving_eur_month"].sum())
print(analysis["saving_eur_month"].mean())
```

::: {.terminal-output .fragment}
```{.text code-line-numbers="false"}
1050
262.5
```
:::

**Total:** EUR 1,050 per month across four households.\
**Mean:** EUR 262.50 per household per month.

::: {.notes}
Clock 42:00–44:00 (2 minutes). Hand check 200 + 400 + 500 - 50 = 1050, then divide by 4.
These describe the four invented records, not the country or all households.
Missing values affect denominators in real datasets; inspect them explicitly
before interpreting an average.
:::

## Check identifiers and missing inputs

```python
print(households["household_id"].is_unique)
print(households.isna().sum().sum())

assert households["household_id"].is_unique
assert households["income_eur_month"].notna().all()
```

::: {.terminal-output .fragment}
```{.text code-line-numbers="false"}
True
0
```
:::

The fixture has unique IDs and no missing cells. A failed check is a reason to investigate.

::: {.notes}
Clock 44:00–47:00 (3 minutes). Explain isna as a table of missing-value indicators. The first
sum counts by column; the second sums those counts. In a real dataset an ID
may repeat across years, so define the observation key first. Do not drop rows
or replace missing values with zero just to make a check pass.
:::

## Calculate income per person

```python
assert (analysis["household_size"] > 0).all()
analysis["income_per_person"] = (
    analysis["income_eur_month"] / analysis["household_size"]
)

print(analysis["income_per_person"].round(2).to_list())
```

::: {.terminal-output .fragment}
```{.text code-line-numbers="false"}
[1000.0, 600.0, 666.67, 400.0]
```
:::

Check the denominator **before dividing**. Rounding here is for the display;
the stored analysis column keeps the calculated precision.

::: {.notes}
Clock 47:00–49:00 (2 minutes). Household sizes are 1, 2, 3 and 2. This is a household's income
divided by its persons; it is a different quantity from the original household
income. The positive-size check is appropriate for the supplied fixture and
the intended definition.
:::

## Save a derived result in `outputs/`

```python
output_path = Path("outputs/household_saving.csv")
output_path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

columns = ["household_id", "saving_eur_month"]
analysis[columns].to_csv(output_path, index=False)
print(output_path.is_file())
```

::: {.terminal-output .fragment}
```{.text code-line-numbers="false"}
True
```
:::

`index=False` omits pandas' row index. The household ID remains an explicit column.

::: {.notes}
Clock 54:00–56:00 (2 minutes). Name the output path aloud and contrast it with data/raw.
The directory creation is supplied standard-library scaffolding. Never save
this analysis over data/raw/households.csv. Generated outputs are ignored by
Git in this repository; the source code and raw teaching fixture are tracked.
:::
